comments.text:
率直なフィードバック、ほんとにありがとう。🙏

ちょっとだけ補足させてほしいんだけど、この動画の中でAIで作ったカットはたった1つだけで、長さも4秒間なんだ。なんでかっていうと、その状況をちゃんと伝えられる実際の映像がどうしても見つからなくて、仕方なく視覚的な補助として使った感じ。それ以外のカットは全部実際の映像で、情報も信頼できるソースをもとにしてるよ。

でも、たとえ4秒でもAIが入ってると混乱させたり、信頼を損ねちゃうってのはその通りだと思う。そこはこっちのミスで、ほんとにごめんね。😔

ただ、チームのみんなが企画考えて、脚本書いて、撮影して、編集して……って一生懸命やってきたのが、たった1つの短いカットだけで判断されちゃうのは、やっぱりちょっと悲しい気持ちもあるんだよね。

そもそもこの動画の目的は、日本の地震対策技術を伝えることであって、むしろ日本が地震を乗り越えてきたすごさを称えて、そこから人類が学べる教訓を残したいっていう思いで作ってるんだ。全部、ポジティブなこと、社会や世界にとって良いことを届けたいっていう気持ちからやってる。そこだけはわかってほしいな。

この意見はすごく真剣に受け止めてる。これからはもっと慎重にするし、実際の映像と確かな情報を優先するようにする。それから、どうしてもAIを使わなきゃいけない時は、誤解されないようにちゃんとその旨を表示するようにするね。

指摘してくれて、本当にありがとう。こういうのが届けられる側としてすごく成長させてもらえるよ。❤️

comments.text: Japan's earthquake technology feels less like fighting nature and more like learning its rhythm. It's hard to beat an opponent, but it's possible to understand one.

comments.author: @WayneScottHall
comments.text: The best safety systems are like good Wi-Fi—you only notice them when they're gone. Invisible engineering deserves more appreciation than it usually gets.

comments.author: @jacoIbfoster
comments.text: You can't negotiate with tectonic plates, but you can negotiate with physics. Japan seems to have become very fluent in that language.

comments.author: @edwarVdhernandez
comments.text: A skyscraper standing after a major earthquake is basically saying, "Thanks for the workout. See you next time." That's confidence earned, not borrowed.

comments.author: @jasonlee1992
comments.text: This documentary proves that science isn't boring. Sometimes it looks like an entire skyline politely refusing to fall over.

comments.author: @JustinMarieKing
comments.text: Flexibility gets criticized until the ground starts shaking. Then suddenly everyone appreciates a building that knows how to stay calm.

comments.author: @LawrencePatrickWilliams
comments.text: Building in Japan must feel like taking a test where the teacher never announces the exam date. Preparation isn't optional—it's the entire strategy.

comments.author: @VincentKeithGonzalez
comments.text: I love how the biggest heroes in this documentary are mostly invisible. Nobody applauds a base isolator—until the day it quietly saves thousands of lives.

comments.author: @gregorycruz2008
comments.text: Japan treats earthquakes like difficult weather instead of impossible monsters. Respect the danger, prepare wisely, and never assume today will be easy.

comments.author: @ethanmorris2004
comments.text: Ancient builders and modern engineers seem to agree on one thing: surviving tomorrow matters more than showing off today.

comments.author: @steventaOylor
comments.text: The strongest lesson here isn't concrete or steel. It's humility. The earth moves whenever it wants, so smart engineers design around reality instead of ego.

comments.author: @Kenneth-Lewis
comments.text: Every earthquake is another reminder that Mother Nature always has the final vote. The best engineers simply make sure the meeting ends with fewer disasters.

comments.author: @JerryRussellRamirez
comments.text: Watching tuned mass dampers work is like seeing a building hire its own personal therapist. "Take a deep breath... don't overreact... keep your balance."

comments.author: @KeithSamuelMurphy
comments.text: It's funny that millions trust giant rubber bearings under skyscrapers every day without thinking twice. Sometimes the quietest inventions protect the loudest cities.

comments.author: @BryanEugeneRodriguez
comments.text: The real miracle is not that Japanese buildings never suffer damage. It is that engineers continuously study every failure and improve the next generation of structures. Humility may be the most important material in earthquake-resistant construction.

comments.author: @ScottBruceWilson
comments.text: Japan’s seismic technology proves that resilience is not one invention. It is a network of dampers, flexible joints, isolation systems, emergency planning, and lessons learned from previous disasters—because concrete alone does not have a backup plan.

comments.author: @Ralph-Ross
comments.text: These engineers design towers as if the planet were an unpredictable neighbor who occasionally starts construction at midnight. You cannot control the noise, but you can reinforce the walls and prepare for the next disturbance.

comments.author: @KennethRandyJames
comments.text: Watching a skyscraper sway can feel unsettling, but movement is often evidence that the safety system is working. A building that refuses to bend may look brave for a few seconds and become a cautionary documentary afterward.

comments.author: @petergeoGrgebrown
comments.text: The smartest part of Japan’s approach is accepting that another major earthquake will eventually happen. That may sound pessimistic, but planning for reality is usually safer than building cheaply and hoping geology develops better manners.

comments.author: @waynewright2008
comments.text: Japanese earthquake engineering feels like architectural judo. Instead of trying to overpower nature, buildings redirect its force—and the earthquake probably leaves wondering how it lost a match against rubber bearings.

comments.author: @jacoBbgomez
comments.text: Base isolation is basically putting an entire building on high-tech sneakers. The ground may throw a tantrum, but the structure gets enough cushioning to avoid joining the drama.

comments.author: @JeffreyRonaldKing
comments.text: Flexible underground pipelines may not look as glamorous as Tokyo’s skyline, but they are the quiet workers keeping water, gas, and transportation systems alive. Every disaster movie needs heroes, and apparently some of them are buried beneath the sidewalk.

comments.author: @josepharthurperezU
comments.text: Japan cannot prevent tectonic plates from moving, so it focuses on controlling the consequences. That is a useful life lesson: you cannot always stop the problem, but you can improve how your system responds to it.

comments.author: @Sjustinhill
comments.text: A tuned mass damper is like having a giant, extremely calm passenger inside the tower who leans in the opposite direction whenever the building begins to panic. That is impressive emotional support for architecture.

comments.author: @LarryRichardBaker
comments.text: Most people assume strength means refusing to move. Japanese engineers understand that a rigid building during an earthquake can be like a stubborn tree in a hurricane—very confident right before becoming firewood.

comments.author: @brandonchavezB
comments.text: Base isolation is basically putting an entire building on high-tech sneakers. The ground may throw a tantrum, but the structure gets enough cushioning to avoid joining the drama.

comments.author: @albertpeterson1995
comments.text: Japan’s skyscrapers handle earthquakes like experienced surfers handle giant waves: they do not waste energy arguing with the ocean. They move, recover, and remain standing while gravity checks the engineering calculations one more time.

comments.author: @StephenRichardPhillips
comments.text: If earthquakes are nature shaking the table, Japan has spent generations figuring out how to keep the glasses from falling. Not magic, just physics, preparation, and a lot of engineering homework.

comments.author: @BrandonAlanReyes
comments.text: These systems deserve praise because they are designed around reality rather than optimism. The ground will move eventually, so the question becomes how intelligently the structure responds.

comments.author: @kylehuEghes
comments.text: Japan’s earthquake technology is basically a reminder that smart engineering often happens long before the emergency. The best rescue can sometimes be damage that never happens.

comments.author: @robertbrooks1992
comments.text: Watching this makes me appreciate building codes differently. They may look like boring paperwork until you realize some regulations are written from decades of hard-earned lessons.

comments.author: @BradleyChristopherEvans
comments.text: The most interesting part is not that Japanese buildings are indestructible—they are not. It is how engineers manage risk through layers of design instead of relying on one miracle solution.

comments.author: @DavidJoshuaLewis
comments.text: Nature does not care how expensive the building is, which makes earthquake engineering such a humbling subject. Every skyscraper still has to obey the same laws of physics.

comments.author: @stephenharris2001
comments.text: This is a great example of technology being impressive without needing to look futuristic. Rubber bearings and dampers may not resemble science fiction, but their physics certainly earns respect.

comments.author: @JoseRussellWilson
comments.text: Japan’s infrastructure feels like a chess player thinking several moves ahead. The earthquake makes the first move, but engineers have spent decades studying the possible responses.

comments.author: @JustinBillyLee
comments.text: Earthquake engineering might be one of the few fields where making a building move can actually mean you designed it correctly. Physics has an interesting sense of humor.

comments.author: @GeorgeBrianMyers

comments.author: @rQandyflores

comments.author: @ScottChristopherMorris
comments.text: The documentary shows why preparation matters more than confidence. Saying “that probably will not happen” is cheap; designing for what happens when it does is engineering.

comments.text:
イオンモール熊本の崩壊は地震が原因ではない」という声があります。では、ちょっとお聞きしたいのですが、地震がガス漏れを引き起こし、そのガスが爆発してイオンモールが崩壊したとしたら、原因は何ですか？

皆さんの論理でいくと、こうなります。
地震 → ガス漏れ → ガス爆発 → 建物崩壊 → 下敷きになる → 呼吸ができなくなる → 死亡。

では、この場合の死因は「呼吸ができなくなったこと」なのか、それとも「地震」なのか？

私は、直接のきっかけは地震にあると考えます。もちろん、爆発が直接の死因であることは事実です。しかし、その爆発を引き起こしたのは地震です。原因を「爆発」だけに限定してしまうと、同じことが今後も繰り返されるリスクを見逃してしまうのではないでしょうか。

comments.text:
Thanks for the honest feedback – I really appreciate it. 🙏

Just to clarify: throughout this entire video, we used exactly ONE AI-generated shot, lasting only 4 seconds. The reason is simple – we couldn't find any real footage that clearly depicted that specific situation, so we used it as a temporary visual aid to help get the point across. Every other shot in the video is real footage, and all the information comes from credible sources.

That said, I completely agree that even 4 seconds of AI can cause confusion and hurt trust. That's on us, and I sincerely apologize. 😔

What stings a little is seeing the hard work our entire team put into the concept, scripting, staging, and editing get judged solely on that one brief moment. We genuinely pour our hearts into delivering valuable, truthful content for our viewers.

Going forward, I'm taking this seriously. We'll be much more careful, prioritize real footage and verified information, and clearly label any AI-generated content if we absolutely have to use it – so there's zero room for misunderstanding.

Thanks again for calling this out. It truly helps us get better. ❤️

replies.text: ご指摘ありがとうございます。この動画は、実際の映像を中心に構成しており、AI生成の画像は1カ所のみ（視覚的な補助として）使用しております。情報の根幹は信頼できる公的機関や報道に基づいており、事実を歪める意図はございません。ご不明な点がございましたら、具体的にお知らせいただければ幸いです。

comments.author: @ceploday
comments.text: とても良い動画です。

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text:
ありがとうございます！そう言っていただけて嬉しいです。特にどのシーンがお気に召しましたか？
こうした温かいコメントが本当に励みになります。いただいた言葉を忘れず、これからも良い動画を作っていきますね。ありがとうございます！

comments.author: @rs646dd
comments.text: 1981年6月施行の新耐震基準以前の建物が多くあるのが問題だ。首都圏で大地震が起こった場合の想定死者数は政府の試算では約18000人、関東大震災（1923）での死者数は約105000人でした。

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text: おっしゃる通りですね。旧耐震基準の建物がまだ多く残っているのは大きなリスクです。政府の試算では、首都直下地震で約18,000人の死者が見込まれていますが、これは建物の耐震化が進んだ場合の数字であり、対策が遅れればさらに増える可能性があります。一方で、1923年の関東大震災では約10万5千人が亡くなっており、当時と比べると耐震技術は格段に進歩しましたが、それでもなお課題は山積みです。特に、木造住宅密集地や旧耐震基準のビルの耐震改修が急務だと思います。この問題について、どのような対策が最も効果的だとお考えですか？

comments.author: @nicholasdRavis
comments.text: Base isolation is like giving a building really expensive shock absorbers. My car complains about potholes while entire Japanese towers are preparing for tectonic plates.

comments.author: @eugenegarygarciPa
comments.text: Perhaps the biggest lesson is that resilience happens long before a disaster arrives. Research labs, building codes, simulations, inspections, and infrastructure upgrades aren’t dramatic, but preparation rarely waits for dramatic music.

comments.author: @P--f5g
comments.text:
2011年3月11日から地震が多発したように感じる。
世界一の地震の巣の上に世界一のメガシティが立っている。
世界一危険で世界一安全な国？
地震・津波・台風・洪水・大火災・・・自然の力の前では無力。人間に出来る事は災害に備えて逃げる事。

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text: @P--f5g ご意見ありがとうございます。おっしゃる通り、大型バッテリーは発火や爆発のリスクがあり、停電時には充電も難しいという課題がありますね。非常用電源としては、ガス式の発電機やポータブル電源と小型ソーラーパネルの組み合わせなども選択肢になるかもしれません。ご自身ではどのような備えをされているのですか？

replies.author: @P--f5g
replies.text: @VagariousTravel-868 大型バッテリーは爆発規模が大きいので推奨できない。電気が無ければ充電できない。

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text: おっしゃる通りですね。災害時に電気と水が止まることは本当に大きなリスクです。非常用の発電機や水の備蓄はもちろん、モバイルバッテリーや簡易トイレなども準備しておくと安心だと思います。ご自身で備えられているものの中で、特に役立ったものはありますか？

replies.author: @P--f5g
replies.text: @VagariousTravel-868 発電機、燃料、水、アウトドア用品は用意しておきたいですね。電気、水が無ければ生きていけない。

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text: その通りですね。日本は地震の巣の上に立っているため、世界で最も危険な国の一つですが、同時に世界で最も準備が整った国でもあります。自然の力には勝てませんが、備えと迅速な避難で命を守ることができます。この動画で、その備えが特に感じられたシーンはありましたか？

comments.author: @Drichardbrown
comments.text: Japan basically looked at earthquakes and said, “Fine, if the ground wants to move, the building gets permission too.” That is one impressive engineering compromise.

comments.author: @peterherZnandez
comments.text: If buildings could talk, these towers would probably say, “I’m not shaking, I’m dissipating seismic energy.” Engineers really found a sophisticated scientific explanation for something that looks terrifying from the sidewalk.

comments.author: @philipstephenwilliEams
comments.text: Watching a skyscraper sway safely feels like seeing a giant tree in a storm. Flexibility looks scary until you realize stiffness can sometimes be the bigger problem.

comments.author: @austinjonathanpriDce
comments.text: Japan’s seismic technology shows why engineering humility matters. You don’t tell nature what it’s allowed to do; you study what it can do and design accordingly. The planet has seniority in this department.

comments.author: @Trangs_k1-o2w
comments.text: These buildings do not fight the ground; they negotiate with it. Apparently, good engineering is knowing when to stand firm and when to dance a little.

comments.author: @christophRerericruiz
comments.text: The real achievement isn’t making a building earthquake-proof, because absolute safety is difficult to promise. It’s reducing risk through better design, materials, monitoring, construction standards, and continuous learning.

comments.author: @christianlewis2002
comments.text: Japan treats earthquakes like an annoying neighbor who keeps slamming the door: you cannot stop them, but you can design the house so the pictures stay on the wall.

comments.author: @matthewdouglascarter1996
comments.text: People see glass, steel, and impressive skylines. Engineers probably see load paths, acceleration, damping, and a long list of calculations that would make the rest of us quietly close the textbook.

comments.author: @Ykeiththomas
comments.text: Base isolation might be one of engineering’s greatest examples of “work smarter, not harder.” Instead of forcing the entire structure to follow every movement below, engineers reduce how much seismic energy reaches the building.

comments.author: @HaroldAlbertMartin
comments.text: There’s a strange beauty in designing something enormous to be flexible. A tower can weigh thousands of tons yet still need to behave more like bamboo than a brick when the ground starts moving.

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text: @P--f5g まさにその通りだと思います。自然をコントロールすることはできなくても、その動きを理解し、備えることで被害を減らすことはできます。日本はその良い例ですね。この動画の中で、特に学びが多いと感じたシーンはありましたか？

replies.author: @P--f5g
replies.text: @VagariousTravel-868 自然の力の前では無力だが学ぶことはできる。

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text: That's a beautiful way to put it. The contrast is striking—massive structures designed to sway like reeds in the wind. Engineers figured out that rigidity breaks, flexibility survives. It's almost poetic. What other natural forms do you think inspire smart engineering?

comments.author: @HaroldChristopherJohnson
comments.text: Japan didn’t invent earthquakes, but it certainly became one of the world’s most interesting classrooms for studying how structures respond to them. Geography handed out a difficult assignment, and engineers kept improving the answers.

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text: Well said. Japan didn't choose to be on the Ring of Fire, but they chose to learn from it. Every earthquake is a new data point, and they use it to build better. That's what makes their engineering so impressive—they never stop improving. What lesson from Japan's approach do you think other countries could apply to their own challenges?

comments.author: @Ryan_David_Green
comments.text: The fascinating part is how much engineering happens before anything goes wrong. Good disaster preparation is like insurance with equations: nobody celebrates it every morning, but everyone appreciates it when conditions turn serious.

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text: Exactly. The best engineering is the kind you never notice until you need it. It's not flashy, but when things go wrong, it's the only thing that matters. That's why I find this stuff so interesting—it's all invisible work that saves lives.

comments.author: @ronaldpeSterson
comments.text: Watching these towers handle movement makes my slightly crooked bookshelf feel less like bad furniture and more like experimental seismic engineering. At least that’s what I’m telling myself.

comments.author: @Vgeralddiaz
comments.text: Earthquakes don’t read building codes, but engineers certainly do. Every improvement in seismic standards represents another attempt to turn lessons from past disasters into safer structures for the future.

comments.author: @noaEhgarcia
comments.text: We usually judge buildings by what we can see, but earthquake safety is often hidden in foundations, joints, dampers, and structural frames. Apparently some of the most impressive architecture lives where tourists never take pictures.

comments.author: @RoyBradleyJackson
comments.text: Japanese seismic engineering feels like architectural martial arts: don’t simply resist the force, redirect and absorb it. The buildings aren’t tougher than the planet; they’re designed to respond more intelligently.

comments.author: @BryanPaulRamirez
comments.text: A skyscraper designed to sway sounds terrifying until you realize the alternative is expecting thousands of tons of concrete to argue with tectonic plates. Suddenly flexibility seems like the sensible option.

comments.author: @HaroldVincentBrown
comments.text: Nature brings the earthquake, engineers bring the homework. Decades of research, testing, and improved building codes show that resilience is usually built through preparation rather than one spectacular invention.

comments.author: @RonaldCharlesHarris
comments.text: Somewhere beneath a beautiful Japanese tower, giant rubber bearings are quietly doing more important work than half the things advertised on the building’s brochure. The best technology doesn’t always need attention.

comments.author: @RaymondPhilipCampbell
comments.text: These buildings remind me of experienced sailors: they survive rough conditions not by refusing to move, but by moving intelligently with the forces around them. That’s physics turned into architecture.
